description: Walking a binary is linear: the rest of a shared binary is a view (Heap::alloc_bitstring_suffix), and fz-sc8.208 (cursor) makes a byte walk allocate nothing per step. Appending with a <> b is linear once fz-nml.2 (PR #617) lands: it writes into a's spare room when a ends where its buffer's bytes end and only the owning process appends (acc <> x x1000: 936 buffers / 498,420 B became 4 / 1,972 B). What remains quadratic is the construction form <<acc::binary, x::binary>>: it builds a fresh binary each time and copies the whole accumulator, so a loop building output that way costs O(n^2) off-heap bytes. BEAM appends in place for this form as well, when the first segment is a writable binary that owns its buffer's end. Probe first: build a 10,000-byte binary with <<acc::binary, <<c>>::binary>> and count shared_bin_bytes per step (Process.heap_alloc_stats) on interp, run and build, against the same loop written with <>. Prediction: about 5,000 bytes per step for the construction form, a constant for <>. Acceptance: both forms share one append authority (the fz-nml.2 room path) and an allocation fixture pins them equal. Needs a proposal page. Old probe: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-j5n-Workspace-fz-xxd13-build/d6960461-b7a2-4585-a9e7-9f2477e57ee2/scratchpad/slow/s3.fz.

comments.text: Constraint from the GC session (read on develop, runtime/src/heap/imp.rs:963-1001 alloc_concatenation): a SharedBin buffer is never reallocated or swapped; nothing assigns bytes_ptr after creation. In-place append happens only when right.len() <= spare() of the fixed capacity; otherwise a NEW SharedBin with room total*2 is allocated (the GrownBuffer site). The page should keep this: grow means a new block, never a realloc. GC has a pending proposal (with the user) to lay a SharedBin out as one block, header then bytes then room, which relies on it.
Related: fz-9x7.25 lays a SharedBin out as one block (header, bytes, room). This ticket's page must keep 'grow means a new block, never a realloc'.

title: Walking or building a binary costs time linear in its length
